power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Wastewater metagenomic sequencing theoretically characterizes all nucleic acids in a sample, but whether sequencing reads reflect transmission dynamics of circulating viruses in the contributing community is unknown.
We evaluated if wastewater metagenomic sequencing data can be used to reconstruct transmission dynamics of endemic, routinely circulating viruses.

Using deep, untargeted wastewater metagenomic sequencing data from four locations in the United States, we generated quantitative estimates of transmission dynamics (time-varying growth rate and effective reproduction number) within a Bayesian framework for widely monitored viruses.
Across locations and viruses, estimates were statistically concordant with those derived from clinical surveillance and polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based wastewater monitoring data.

Furthermore, we estimated growth rate from wastewater metagenomic sequencing data for numerous viruses not otherwise widely monitored, demonstrating the data expands the targets that can feasibly be monitored in parallel.

The COVID-19 pandemic significantly expanded the use of wastewater monitoring for infectious disease surveillance.

Before the pandemic, wastewater monitoring was primarily used for binary pathogen detection and notably to support polio eradication efforts. 1 During the pandemic, studies demonstrated that wastewater concentrations of SARS-CoV-2 RNA reflect COVID-19 incidence, 2, 3 bringing mainstream attention to its use for quantitatively tracking disease transmission dynamics.

text.text: Wastewater monitoring has since expanded to a myriad of pathogens-including other respiratory viruses, 4 enteric viruses, 5 fungi, 6 bacteria, 7, 8 and arboviruses https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?4UTd8g -along with other purposes, such as tracking variants, 11, 12 identifying trends, 13 evaluating policies and nonpharmaceutical interventions, 14, 15 and inferring seasonal characteristics and drivers. [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] Presently, most wastewater monitoring efforts use quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based methods to detect prespecified, known viruses. 21 These "targeted" methods have shown significant utility for detecting and quantitatively tracking known pathogens.

text.text: However, because assay design requires prior knowledge of the target genome sequence, targeted approaches are neither suited to detect novel or rapidly evolving pathogens nor feasibly monitor the full diversity of viruses in wastewater.
By contrast, metagenomic sequencing characterizes nucleic acids across a sample without needing to prespecify targets.
Shotgun metagenomic sequencing methods, referred to here as "untargeted" wastewater monitoring, involves sequencing all genomic material present in a wastewater sample.

Nucleic acids from human pathogenic viruses comprise a small fraction of this material, however, so sensitive and consistent detection requires substantial sequencing depth or high total sequencing reads per sample. 22 Nonetheless, declining sequencing costs have increased feasibility for scaling wastewater metagenomic sequencing with most attention focusing on its capability to detect novel or unexpected pathogens.
text.formatted: Nucleic acids from human pathogenic viruses comprise a small fraction of this material, however, so sensitive and consistent detection requires substantial sequencing depth or high total sequencing reads per sample. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22</ref> Nonetheless, declining sequencing costs have increased feasibility for scaling wastewater metagenomic sequencing with most attention focusing on its capability to detect novel or unexpected pathogens.

text.text: In addition to its ability to detect novel or unexpected pathogens, wastewater metagenomic sequencing generates billions of reads of expected, endemic targets, meaning the data are also positioned to provide broader public health value.

Virus-specific normalized read abundance from untargeted wastewater monitoring data have been shown to temporally correlate with targeted wastewater monitoring and clinical surveillance data for human pathogenic viruses, 23, 24 suggesting that wastewater metagenomic sequencing may be used to infer quantitative transmission dynamics of both widely-surveilled (e.g., SARS-CoV-2) and under-surveilled (e.g., rhinovirus) pathogens.
text.formatted: Virus-specific normalized read abundance from untargeted wastewater monitoring data have been shown to temporally correlate with targeted wastewater monitoring and clinical surveillance data for human pathogenic viruses, <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">24</ref> suggesting that wastewater metagenomic sequencing may be used to infer quantitative transmission dynamics of both widely-surveilled (e.g., SARS-CoV-2) and under-surveilled (e.g., rhinovirus) pathogens.

text.text: If so, wastewater metagenomic sequencing could serve multiple public health functions, including early detection of emerging, unexpected, or hitherto unseen threats and routine, quantitative monitoring of multiple endemic pathogens in parallel.
Whether virus-specific metagenomic read abundance can reliably reconstruct underlying transmission dynamics remains unknown.

Two quantitative statistics widely used to monitor transmission dynamics are the instantaneous epidemic growth rate ( r t ) and effective reproduction number ( R t ). 25, 26 Both r t and R t have been estimated from wastewater monitoring data, although only using data collected via targeted approaches. 27, 28 To our knowledge, no studies have evaluated whether untargeted wastewater monitoring data may be used to reliably infer transmission dynamics (as represented by r t and R t ).
text.formatted: Two quantitative statistics widely used to monitor transmission dynamics are the instantaneous epidemic growth rate ( r t ) and effective reproduction number ( R t ). <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">26</ref> Both r t and R t have been estimated from wastewater monitoring data, although only using data collected via targeted approaches. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">28</ref> To our knowledge, no studies have evaluated whether untargeted wastewater monitoring data may be used to reliably infer transmission dynamics (as represented by r t and R t ).

text.text: In this study, we aimed to assess the use of untargeted wastewater monitoring data for quantitatively tracking pathogen transmission dynamics.

Using data from four distinct sites in the United States, we estimated r t and R t using untargeted wastewater monitoring, targeted wastewater monitoring, and clinical surveillance data for widely-monitored viruses.
We then evaluated concordance among the time-varying estimates of pathogen transmission derived from each data source.
Secondarily, we estimated r t for viruses only with available untargeted wastewater monitoring data to infer the transmission dynamics of less-monitored viruses.
We found that wastewater metagenomic sequencing tracks transmission dynamics concordant with other data sources while expanding the viral targets we can reliably monitor.

We obtained clinical surveillance, targeted wastewater monitoring, and untargeted wastewater monitoring data for various viruses from four sites in the United States ( Fig. 1 ): Boise, Idaho (November 2024-March 2026); Boston, Massachusetts (September 2024-March 2026); Riverside, California (December 2024-March 2026); and Ottumwa, Iowa (February 2025-March 2026).

We obtained weekly totals of disease diagnoses by International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10) code ( Table S1-2 ) from Epic Cosmos within the county or state of sites. 29 For influenza A and B virus (IAV/IBV), we instead obtained weekly totals of positive lab results.

For untargeted wastewater monitoring data, we used weekly virus clade counts normalized by PMMoV clade counts that were scaled to account for sequencing depth.

We derived r t by smoothing time series data using a generalized additive model (GAM), implemented in a Bayesian framework using the mgcv R package, 30 and then calculating the logarithmic derivative of smoothed data. 26 To derive R t , we used the renewal equation model in a Bayesian framework 31 as described by the R package EpiNow2. 32 Refer to the Methods for model specifications, but both approaches derive daily estimates.  21 for rotavirus, HAdV F, and parvovirus B19.

The renewal equation links observed surveillance signals to latent infections in the population via a generative model of transmission and infection-to-reporting and infection-to-shedding delays for clinical and wastewater data sources, respectively.
These viruses had surveillance data from multiple sources, and we obtained sufficient data to inform prior model assumptions-particularly regarding fecal shedding dynamics ( Table S4 ).

Wastewater metagenomic sequencing-or untargeted wastewater monitoring-is particularly well-suited to detect rare, albeit potentially consequential, novel and reemerging threats.
Yet the data simultaneously offer routine public health value as most wastewater metagenomic reads belonging to viruses are of circulating, endemic pathogens.

We demonstrated that untargeted wastewater monitoring may be used to quantitatively track transmission dynamics of routinely detected viruses while expanding the range of targets that may be reliably monitored.

Estimates of growth rate ( r t ) and effective reproduction number ( R t ) derived from untargeted wastewater monitoring data were significantly concordant with those derived from clinical data and targeted, PCR-based wastewater monitoring data.
Moreover, untargeted wastewater monitoring data covered more viral targets than other data sources, allowing transmission dynamics to be inferred for a wider number of targets.
Across distinct locations and viruses, we provided evidence that untargeted wastewater monitoring can recapitulate R t and r t as derived from clinical and targeted wastewater monitoring.

The timing and magnitude of peak R t and r t estimates derived from untargeted wastewater monitoring data were overall relatively similar as when derived from other data sources during periods of increasing disease transmission.

In addition, the relative timing of observed peak R t values derived from untargeted wastewater monitoring data during the 2024-25 season aligned with established temporal patterns based on historic clinical and targeted wastewater monitoring data.

RSV typically peaks first, followed by IAV then IBV which we observed. 19, 34 The seasonality of SARS-CoV-2 is not as established but in past years has had a wintertime peak coinciding with RSV and influenza; 16, 19 we observed a peak in SARS-CoV-2 R t between that of RSV and influenza.

text.text: Our Bayesian permutation analysis then provided statistical evidence that the observed similarities in R t and r t estimates derived from untargeted wastewater monitoring and other data sources were significant.

Other studies have calculated metrics similar to MAE, AOB, and correlation to assess similarity between two derived time series, although only between point estimates. 27, 39, 40 By using permutation within a Bayesian framework, we not only quantified the numerical discrepancy, agreement on epidemic direction, and temporal association between two time series but further provided statistical evidence that the observed metrics were significantly different than had there been no relationship between the two time series.

text.text: Nonetheless, there are shortcomings to our statistical approach which may explain why not all tests were significant.
First, some clinical data were sparse at the county level so we used state-level data instead ( Table S2 ).
text.formatted: First, some clinical data were sparse at the county level so we used state-level data instead ( Table <ref type="table">S2</ref> ).

text.text: Lack of concordance between estimates from untargeted wastewater monitoring and clinical data may be attributed to geographic differences between the localized and statewide population.
Second, the duration of targeted wastewater monitoring was shorter than other data sources.

R t estimates towards the end of the time window of a data source are less reliable; therefore, the end date of targeted wastewater monitoring occurring before that of clinical surveillance and untargeted wastewater monitoring data may have contributed to estimates derived from targeted wastewater monitoring sometimes lacking concordance with other data sources.
Third, the permutation testing we adopted to infer significance of similarity depends on temporal variation in the data.
Permuting a time series with its own time points randomizes that variation and enables principled construction of a null distribution and comparison.
By contrast, time series with relatively low degrees of temporal variation (e.g., those that fluctuate minimally around R t = 1) do not differ much once permuted.
Consequently, achieving significant differentiation between the observed and null posterior distributions is challenging with time series that do not exhibit substantial temporal variation.

Lack of a complete year of concurrent surveillance (aside from Boston) may explain why estimates derived from untargeted wastewater monitoring were not always significantly concordant with other data sources despite visually appearing so.

Lastly, we convolved latent infections to expected case reports using incubation period and reporting delay distributions for clinical data and fecal shedding distributions for wastewater data sources.

While these distributions theoretically account for the delays unique to each data source, meaning inferred peak R t estimates should coincide across data sources, information to deduce these distributions-especially reporting and shedding delay distributions-is sparse.
Lack of reporting and shedding delay data for viruses may further explain why derived R t estimates were not always concordant across data sources.
Most viruses included in this study only had untargeted wastewater monitoring data available.
For the viruses with multiple surveillance sources, estimates from untargeted wastewater monitoring data were overall concordant when compared to other data sources.
Therefore, we derived r t from untargeted wastewater monitoring alone for remaining viruses.
Overall, r t estimates from untargeted wastewater monitoring data aligned with known epidemiological features of these viruses according to historical surveillance ( Table 1 ).

text.text: Because many of these viruses are less prioritized compared to SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and RSV, future work should focus on better understanding the epidemiology of these less-studied viruses.
Wastewater metagenomic sequencing offers a compelling means to do so as it does not rely on testing-seeking behaviors, clinical testing of specimens, or targeted assay design.
For example, Smith et al. 41 retrospectively elucidated seasonal dynamics for a range of targets detected via wastewater metagenomic sequencing data using linear mixed effects models.

text.text: Future studies should build upon this work to develop methods for prospectively identifying levels and trends or seasonal onset, peak, offset, and duration.

Such methods have already been developed for targeted wastewater monitoring data; 13, [16] [17] [18] [19] extending this work to untargeted wastewater monitoring data would greatly expand its utility.

text.text: While our study highlights a compelling use of wastewater metagenomic sequencing, it has limitations.
Foremost, longitudinal shedding concentration data are not available for most viruses.
Viruses rarely detected may be widely present in a population but not shed into wastewater in detectable quantities.
Moreover, viruses with low read counts may be widely present but shed in low quantities (e.g., respiratory viruses), making it more challenging to differentiate signal from noise.

Second, metagenomic read counts are influenced by genome size, nucleic acid extraction efficiency, and sequencing depth, and it is possible reads may be incorrectly mapped to reference genomes or that reference genomes may be sparse.
However, estimates derived from untargeted wastewater monitoring were concordant with those derived from the other data sources for the sequencing depth and normalization used.

Estimation tools for targeted wastewater monitoring data exist but are often data intensive, requiring PCR and sample metadata we did not have. 39, 51, 52 No tools for untargeted wastewater monitoring data yet exist but could account for sequencing depth and data processing time lags unique to untargeted wastewater monitoring data.

text.text: Notwithstanding, our study is the first of our knowledge to estimate r t and R t from untargeted wastewater monitoring data and evaluate concordance with existing surveillance data using permutation analysis within a Bayesian framework.
We highlight a practical use case for wastewater metagenomic reads for tracking transmission dynamics of known viruses, including those not widely monitored via other surveillance means.

As interest and planned investment in wastewater metagenomic sequencing grows nationally, our work emphasizes that broader public health value that may be derived from the data, ranging from early detection of novel pathogens to routine surveillance of endemic pathogens.

text.text: GAMs implemented using the mgcv R package have an empirical Bayesian interpretation as the smoothing parameter estimated via REML uses a frequentist approach and the uncertainty calculation to obtain credible intervals (CrIs) uses a Bayesian approach.
Thus, for each GAM fit, we extracted 1,000 posterior draws and estimated the median and 90% CrI each day to produce a smoothed time series.
Next, to estimate daily r t from each smoothed time series, we approximated the logarithmic derivative of the smoothed time series S t using Equation 1 with a daily time step.
We approximated the logarithmic derivative each day using all 1,000 posterior draws to calculate the median and 90% CrI of the r t estimate.
Estimating R t requires an epidemiological model to link an observed surveillance signal to latent infections in the population.
Therefore, for each location, we estimated R t only for viruses with sufficient data to inform model parameters: SARS-CoV-2, IAV, IBV, RSV, NoV, and rotavirus.

For each virus, we estimated R t from each available surveillance data source using the renewal equation model in a Bayesian framework, as described by the R package EpiNow2 ( Equation 2 ). 31, 32 The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) similarly used EpiNow2 to estimate R t from emergency department visit data between 2022-May 2026. 59 According to the renewal equation, latent infections each day I t are given by the total infectiousness of infected individuals on day t , multiplied by the effective reproduction number R t .

text.text: Namely, D t ww and C t ww instead represent the expected and observed wastewater signal, respectively, arising from latent infections I t in this adapted framework ( Equation 5-6 ).

The wastewater signal is PMMoV-normalized concentrations of viral nucleic acids using targeted wastewater monitoring data and PMMoV-normalized virus clade counts scaled to account for sequencing depth using untargeted wastewater monitoring data.

EpiNow2 can only handle integer counts; therefore, we multiplied wastewater signals in a time series by a constant factor and rounded such that they represented integer counts analogous to clinical data.

When both clinical and wastewater data were available for a given site and virus, we multiplied wastewater signals by a factor that resulted in the median rounded wastewater signal being on the same order of magnitude as the median clinical count.

When only wastewater data were available, we multiplied wastewater signals so the median rounded wastewater signal was above one and on the same order of magnitude as the other wastewater data source, if both wastewater data sources were available.
R t is primarily affected by relative changes in the surveillance signal rather than absolute changes.
Thus, R t estimates are robust to the choice of multiplication factor (see Fig. S33 for a comparison of different choices of this multiplication factor).

text.text: Assessing concordance in time-varying estimates derived from different surveillance data sources Specifically, for both r t and R t , we calculated MAE, AOB, and Kendall's tau between all pairs of posterior draws derived from data source a and b .
Doing so generated an observed posterior distribution for each concordance metric and each pair of data sources.
Since each surveillance data source has unique biases and limitations, no surveillance data source represents a gold standard.

Therefore, to assess whether two surveillance data sources generated significantly similar r t and R t estimates than would be expected by random chance, we generated null posterior distributions for each pair of data sources using Bayesian permutation analysis.
Specifically, we permuted each posterior draw across time points of data source b and recalculated each metric between data source a and b perm , generating null posterior distributions.

For each pair of data sources and concordance metric, the null posterior distribution represented the posterior distribution under a null hypothesis of no temporal concordance or relationship between the two data sources.
We then calculated Bayesian permutation p values which represent the proportion of posterior draws in which the null scenario was more similar than the observed scenario.
For MAE, values closer to 0 indicate similarity, so we calculated permutation p values as the proportion of null draw pairs less than observed draw pairs.
In contrast, AOB and tau coefficients closer to 1 indicate similarity; we calculated permutation p values as the proportion of null draw pairs greater than observed draw pairs.

We interpreted permutation p values < 0.05 as suggesting significant concordance between two data sources as this indicated the null hypothesis was not rejected in less than 5% of posterior draw pairs.

Estimating time-varying effective reproduction number ( R t )
When we estimated daily r t and R t from two or more surveillance data sources, we assessed concordance among the time-varying estimates between all pairs of data sources.
We used three complementary concordance metrics: (1) mean absolute error (MAE), (2) agreement on binary (AOB), and (3) correlation.
MAE ( Equation7) quantifies numerical agreement between two time series.

AOB ( Equation8) assesses agreement on epidemic direction between two time series; we used thresholds ɸ of 0 (AOB0) and 1 (AOB1) for r t and R t , respectively, as these thresholds are used to assess whether an epidemic is growing or shrinking for each metric.
In Equations 7-8 , y represents the derived time-varying estimate each day t from data source a and b and n represents the total number of concurrent days between these same data sources.
Correlation evaluates whether two time series are temporally associated.
Given that time series estimates may not always be normally distributed, we used Kendall's tau correlation to calculate correlation coefficients.

Positive tau values indicate positive temporal association between the daily time-varying estimates derived from data source a and b whereas negative tau values indicate negative temporal association.
